Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

Electrograms recorded inside the heart carry more detail than the surface ECG, and mapping systems
collect thousands of them, each tied to a place on the heart. AI is used on both: on single
electrograms or short recordings, to label patterns such as rotational activation [@alhusseini2020]
or driver sites [@zolotarev2020]; and on whole maps, where points are linked by the mesh and a
graph network can learn from neighbours [@saluja2024]. One AI tool has been tested in a randomized
trial: ablation guided by an algorithm that detects spatiotemporal electrogram dispersion, added to
pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), against PVI alone [@deisenhofer2025]. This module derives graph
convolution on a mapping mesh, the metrics for judging a predicted region, and losses for rare
targets, and it shows how a split by window rather than by patient overstates accuracy on real
intracardiac recordings.

## From the field

- **Experts label, then networks learn.** A Stanford team labeled 175,000 bi-atrial activation
  grids from 35 patients for rotational activation (expert agreement κ = 0.79) and trained a
  convolutional network that reached 95.0% accuracy on a separate test set of 50,000 grids
  [@alhusseini2020]. Labels from experts carry their disagreement into the model (m35).
- **Ground truth from another modality.** In explanted human atria, optical mapping defined which
  electrodes sat on a driver. Averaging features over each electrode's 8 neighbours improved
  classification over single electrograms [@zolotarev2020], an early form of what graph networks do.
- **Graphs fit mapping data.** A graph convolutional network on electroanatomic maps of 29
  scar-related atrial tachycardias predicted isthmus areas with a median centroid distance of 7.3 mm
  in the test group, but a mean Dice overlap of only 13.9% [@saluja2024]. The two metrics answer
  different questions (demo m39-d2).
- **Rare targets need different metrics.** A 1-D network for ganglionated plexi on bipolar
  electrograms, with target windows near 3.5% of the data and trained with a focal loss, had a recall
  of 0.85 but a precision of 0.09 on validation [@guler2026].
- **Signals and outcomes.** Stanford groups have combined intracardiac electrograms, the ECG and
  clinical data to predict AF recurrence after ablation [@tang2022], and found that acute AF
  termination and 1-year success were predicted by different features [@ganesan2025].
- **Unsupervised structure.** Gaussian mixtures fitted to the whole distribution of left atrial
  voltages split one cohort into milder and more severe atrial cardiomyopathy without a fixed
  threshold [@huttelmaier2026].

## Derivations

Symbols: a mesh with $n$ vertices, adjacency $A$ ($A_{ij} = 1$ when vertices $i$ and $j$ share an
edge), degree $d_i$, feature matrix $X$ ($n \times f$), weights $W$, $p$ a predicted probability,
$y$ a label, $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ the focal-loss parameters.

### Graph convolution on a mapping mesh

A mapping system's points live on a triangle mesh. A **graph convolution** layer updates every
vertex from itself and its neighbours [@kipf2017]:

$$
H' = \sigma\!\left(\hat A H W\right), \qquad
\hat A = \tilde D^{-1/2}\,(A + I)\,\tilde D^{-1/2}
$$ {#eq-m39-gcn}

where $\tilde D$ is the diagonal matrix of degrees of $A + I$ and $\sigma$ a nonlinearity such as
ReLU. Each vertex takes a weighted average of its own features and its neighbours', $\hat A_{ij} =
1/\sqrt{\tilde d_i \tilde d_j}$, then mixes the feature channels with $W$, which is shared by all
vertices. After $L$ layers a vertex depends only on vertices within $L$ edges: the graph version of
the receptive field in m37.

Without $W$ and $\sigma$, $\hat A$ is a smoothing operator. It is symmetric, its eigenvalues lie in
$(-1, 1]$, and the eigenvalue 1 belongs to

$$
\hat A\, \mathbf v = \mathbf v, \qquad v_i \propto \sqrt{\tilde d_i}
$$ {#eq-m39-smoothing}

which follows from $\sum_j \hat A_{ij}\sqrt{\tilde d_j} = \sum_{j \in \{i\} \cup N(i)} 1/\sqrt{\tilde d_i}
= \sqrt{\tilde d_i}$. Repeated layers pull every map towards $\mathbf v$: they keep slow spatial
variation and remove fast variation, a low-pass filter on the mesh (the mesh Laplacian of m06 in
another form). A few layers average noise away; too many blur small targets.

$\mathbf v$ is constant only when every vertex has the same degree. The course's grid mesh
alternates interior points with 4 and 8 neighbours, so its $\mathbf v$ is a fine checkerboard with
values in the ratio $\sqrt{5} : \sqrt{9}$, and that pattern appears in the right panel of the demo
below after a few layers. It comes from the normalization, not from noise. The row-normalized
operator $\tilde D^{-1}(A + I)$ maps a constant map to itself; the symmetric form is the one
@kipf2017 used.

::: {.demo #m39-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m39-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m39-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m39-d1-graph-smoothing.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Each layer applies $\hat A$ of @eq-m39-gcn with no learned weights, exactly. The mesh is the
  course's triangulated grid (`epml.mapping.plane_mesh`), 31 by 31 points 2 mm apart.
- The map holds 1.0 outside a disc and 0.2 inside, plus noise with a fixed random pattern. These are
  illustrative values in arbitrary units, not voltages.
- The fine checkerboard in the right panel is the fixed point of @eq-m39-smoothing on this mesh,
  whose points have 4 or 8 neighbours.
- What would change the result: learned weights choose what to keep; real meshes have uneven point
  density, so "L edges" means different distances in different places.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A graph-convolution layer is a weighted neighbour average followed by a shared channel mix.
- After $L$ layers a vertex sees its $L$-edge neighbourhood.
- Stacked layers low-pass filter the map: they remove noise and, eventually, small targets.

### Judging a predicted region

A model that marks part of a map as a target can be judged by overlap or by location. The **Dice
coefficient** of a predicted set $P$ and a true set $T$, with area weights on mesh vertices, is

$$
\mathrm{Dice} = \frac{2\,\lvert P \cap T \rvert}{\lvert P \rvert + \lvert T \rvert}
$$ {#eq-m39-dice}

The **centroid distance** is the distance between the centres of $P$ and $T$. For two discs of
radii $R$ and $r$ whose centres are $d$ apart, the overlap has a closed form, the area of a lens:

$$
\lvert P \cap T\rvert = r^2 \cos^{-1}\!\frac{d^2 + r^2 - R^2}{2dr} + R^2 \cos^{-1}\!\frac{d^2 + R^2 - r^2}{2dR}
- \tfrac12\sqrt{(-d + r + R)(d + r - R)(d - r + R)(d + r + R)}
$$ {#eq-m39-lens}

for $\lvert R - r\rvert < d < R + r$; the overlap is the smaller disc when $d \le \lvert R - r\rvert$,
and zero when $d \ge R + r$. With two discs of radius 4 mm, centres 7 mm apart overlap by less than
15%. A small target can be "found" by centroid distance and missed by Dice. Report both.

::: {.demo #m39-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m39-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m39-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m39-d2-dice-centroid.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m39-lens and @eq-m39-dice for two discs on a plane, exact.
- The default distance, 7.3 mm, echoes the median centroid distance reported by @saluja2024; the
  radii are illustrative and are not taken from that study.
- What would change the result: real targets are not discs, and they lie on curved surfaces, where
  distances are geodesic (m06).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Dice measures overlap; centroid distance measures location. They can disagree.
- For small targets, a few millimetres of offset destroys overlap.
- Choose the metric that matches the use: where to look, or what to treat as the target.

### Rare targets

When targets cover a few percent of a map, a model trained with plain cross-entropy can do well on
average by predicting "no target" almost everywhere. Two common fixes change the loss. A weight on
positive examples scales their cross-entropy terms. The **focal loss** also shrinks the loss of
examples the model already gets right [@lin2017focal]:

$$
\mathrm{FL}(p_t) = -\alpha_t\,(1 - p_t)^{\gamma}\,\log p_t
$$ {#eq-m39-focal}

where $p_t$ is the predicted probability of the true class, $\alpha_t = \alpha$ for positives and
$1 - \alpha$ for negatives, and $\gamma \ge 0$. With $\gamma = 0$ it is weighted cross-entropy; with
$\gamma > 0$, an example with $p_t$ near 1 contributes almost nothing. @guler2026 used it with
$\alpha = 0.75$ and $\gamma = 2$.

A loss changes what the model learns, not how it should be judged. With rare targets, report
precision and recall (or the area under the precision–recall curve) rather than only ROC AUC:
precision is the PPV of [m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv) at a low prevalence.

**Key takeaways**

- Rare targets push a model towards "never"; weighting or a focal loss pushes back.
- ROC AUC can look high while precision is low; quote precision and recall.
- The operating threshold, not the loss, decides how many false targets a user sees.

### Structure without labels

Some questions have no labels at all, for example whether a cohort's voltage distributions fall
into groups. A **Gaussian mixture** models values as coming from $K$ normal components with
weights $\pi_k$, means $\mu_k$ and standard deviations $\sigma_k$. The probability that value $x_i$
came from component $k$ is its **responsibility**:

$$
\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k\, \mathcal N(x_i \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} \pi_j\, \mathcal N(x_i \mid \mu_j, \sigma_j)}
$$ {#eq-m39-gmm}

Expectation–maximization alternates between computing $\gamma_{ik}$ and re-estimating each
component from the values weighted by its responsibilities. @huttelmaier2026 used Gaussian mixtures
in this way on left atrial voltage distributions. Clusters are a description of the data; whether
they mean anything for patients needs outside evidence, as that study sought with other markers.

**Key takeaways**

- A mixture assigns each value a probability of belonging to each group.
- Expectation–maximization fits it without labels.
- Clusters need external validation before they mean anything clinical.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**AI-guided ablation of electrogram dispersion.** Spatiotemporal dispersion was first described as
a visually recognizable pattern of electrograms on a multispline catheter, which simulations and
optical mapping linked to the vicinity of AF drivers [@seitz2017]. That study compared dispersion-
guided ablation with a separate validation set treated conventionally, not with a randomized
control.

TAILORED-AF tested an AI algorithm that detects dispersion in a multicentre, randomized,
double-blind trial in drug-refractory persistent AF [@deisenhofer2025]. Against expert annotations,
the algorithm had a ROC AUC of 0.94, reported in the trial's supplement. Patients were randomized to
ablation of dispersion areas plus PVI (n = 187) or PVI alone (n = 183). At 12 months after one
procedure, freedom from documented AF was 88% versus 70%. Freedom from any atrial arrhythmia did not
differ significantly between arms, procedure and ablation times were about twice as long in the
tailored arm, and the composite safety endpoint did not differ. Later analyses looked at women
[@deisenhofer2025women] and at the atrial tachycardias seen after the procedure
[@deisenhofer2025at]. A single-arm study applied the approach to repeat procedures in patients whose
veins remained isolated [@hummel2026].

In the terms of this module and m45:

- **The randomized comparison tests the whole strategy** (AI detection plus extra ablation plus
  PVI) against PVI, not the algorithm alone.
- **Endpoints differ in what they show.** The primary endpoint (AF) favoured the tailored arm; the
  broader endpoint (any atrial arrhythmia) did not differ.
- **Single-arm results depend on selection.** In the repeat-procedure study, many enrolled patients
  left before the primary endpoint, for example because their veins had reconnected
  [@hummel2026].

## How experts think

Before trusting a model that reads electrograms or maps, ask:

1. **Where did the labels come from?** Expert annotation (with its agreement, [@alhusseini2020]),
   another modality such as optical mapping [@zolotarev2020], or the outcome of an ablation?
2. **What was split?** Windows from one recording, points from one map and maps from one patient are
   all correlated. Split by patient (lab part E).
3. **How far does the model look?** A graph network with $L$ layers sees $L$ edges; a per-point model
   sees one point (@eq-m39-gcn).
4. **Which metric matches the use?** Dice for "this is the target", centroid distance for "look
   here" (@eq-m39-dice, @eq-m39-lens), precision and recall for rare targets (@eq-m39-focal).
5. **What did the trial test?** In TAILORED-AF, the comparison was a strategy built on the AI,
   against PVI alone [@deisenhofer2025].

One sentence to keep: **on a map, every point has neighbours; models, splits and metrics must know
it.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Graph convolution (@eq-m39-gcn) | $H' = \sigma(\hat A H W)$, $\hat A = \tilde D^{-1/2}(A+I)\tilde D^{-1/2}$ |
| Smoothing fixed point (@eq-m39-smoothing) | $\hat A\mathbf v = \mathbf v$ for $v_i \propto \sqrt{\tilde d_i}$; eigenvalues in $(-1, 1]$ |
| Dice (@eq-m39-dice) | $2\lvert P\cap T\rvert/(\lvert P\rvert + \lvert T\rvert)$ |
| Lens area (@eq-m39-lens) | Overlap of two discs, radii $R$, $r$, centres $d$ apart |
| Focal loss (@eq-m39-focal) | $-\alpha_t(1-p_t)^\gamma\log p_t$; $\gamma = 0$ gives weighted cross-entropy |
| Mixture responsibility (@eq-m39-gmm) | $\gamma_{ik} = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(x_i)/\sum_j \pi_j\mathcal N_j(x_i)$ |

**Studies in this module**

| Study | What was learned | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @alhusseini2020 | Rotational activation in AF activation grids | Retrospective; separate test set |
| @zolotarev2020 | Driver electrodes, labeled by optical mapping | Ex vivo human atria |
| @saluja2024 | Isthmus areas of scar-related atrial tachycardia (graph network) | Retrospective, 29 tachycardias |
| @guler2026 | Ganglionated plexi from bipolar electrograms | Retrospective, held-out atria |
| @deisenhofer2025 | Strategy: AI-detected dispersion ablation plus PVI vs PVI | Randomized trial |

**Rules of thumb**

- Split by patient; windows and points from one patient are not independent.
- Two to three graph layers smooth noise; more layers blur small targets.
- For rare targets, show the precision–recall curve.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Write one graph-convolution layer and explain each factor.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$H' = \sigma(\hat A H W)$ with $\hat A = \tilde D^{-1/2}(A + I)\tilde D^{-1/2}$ (@eq-m39-gcn). $A + I$ links
each vertex to its neighbours and itself; the degree normalization keeps high-degree vertices from
dominating; $W$ mixes feature channels and is shared by all vertices, so the layer works on meshes of
any size; $\sigma$ adds nonlinearity. After $L$ layers a vertex sees its $L$-edge neighbourhood.

</details>

**Q2. Why does stacking many graph layers wash out a map?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\hat A$ is symmetric with eigenvalues in $(-1, 1]$, and its eigenvector for 1 is $v_i \propto
\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$ (@eq-m39-smoothing). Repeated application shrinks every other component, so the map
tends towards that one shape: high spatial frequencies go first. Noise is removed, but so are small
targets. Demo m39-d1 shows both.

</details>

**Q3. A model's predicted target centre is 7 mm from the true centre. Is that good?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It depends on the target's size and the use. For two discs of radius 4 mm, 7 mm apart, Dice is below
15% (@eq-m39-lens). @saluja2024 reported a median centroid distance of 7.3 mm with a mean Dice of
13.9%. As a pointer to where to map more densely it may help; as a definition of what to ablate it
overlaps the target poorly.

</details>

**Q4. Your positive class is 1% of points. The model's ROC AUC is 0.94. What else do you report?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Precision and recall at the chosen threshold, and the precision–recall curve or its area. At low
prevalence, a modest false-positive rate swamps the true positives, so precision can be low while ROC
AUC looks high; precision is PPV at that prevalence ([m35](m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv)).
@guler2026 is an example: recall 0.85, precision 0.09.

</details>

**Q5. What does the focal loss change, and what does it not change?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It down-weights examples the model already classifies well, by $(1-p_t)^\gamma$, and can weight
classes by $\alpha$ (@eq-m39-focal). Training then concentrates on hard and rare examples. It does not
change how the model should be evaluated, and it does not choose the operating threshold; that is a
separate decision about acceptable false positives.

</details>

**Q6. You have 30-second recordings from 8 patients, 4 catheter positions each, cut into 4-s windows.
How do you split for testing?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

By patient: leave one patient out, train on the others, and rotate. Windows from one recording share
the patient, the catheter contact and the rhythm, so a window-wise split lets the model recognize the
recording instead of the pattern. Lab part E shows the gap on the Intracardiac AF Database.

</details>

**Q7. Why did averaging features over neighbouring electrodes help driver detection?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A driver is a spatial pattern: neighbouring electrodes share evidence for it, while noise at single
electrodes is partly independent. Averaging over the 8 neighbours [@zolotarev2020] raises the signal
relative to the noise, the same idea as one unweighted graph-convolution layer (@eq-m39-gcn).

</details>

**Q8. In TAILORED-AF, what exactly was compared?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Two strategies in drug-refractory persistent AF: ablation of AI-detected dispersion areas plus PVI,
against PVI alone, randomized and double-blind [@deisenhofer2025]. The primary endpoint, freedom from
documented AF at 12 months after one procedure, was 88% versus 70%; freedom from any atrial
arrhythmia did not differ significantly, and procedures took about twice as long in the tailored arm.
The trial tests the strategy, not the algorithm's accuracy on its own.

</details>

**Q9. What does a Gaussian mixture give you that a fixed voltage threshold does not?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A description of the whole distribution: how many groups, their means and spreads, and for each
value a probability of belonging to each group (@eq-m39-gmm). It does not depend on a threshold chosen
in advance [@huttelmaier2026]. It does not tell you that the groups matter clinically; that needs
outside evidence.

</details>

**Q10. A paper reports 95% accuracy for classifying activation grids. What do you check?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

How labels were made and how much experts agreed (κ = 0.79 in @alhusseini2020); whether test grids came
from patients not used in training; class balance; what "95%" counts (grids, not patients); whether
the explanation of the model matched expert rules; and whether anything beyond accuracy was tested,
such as use during procedures.

</details>

**Q11. Why is a graph network a natural fit for mapping data, compared with an image network?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Mapping points sit on a curved surface with uneven density; there is no regular pixel grid. A graph
network works directly on the mesh's connections, shares weights across vertices and handles any
number of points. An image network needs the surface flattened or resampled, which distorts
distances. The lab compares a graph network with a per-point model on the same features.

</details>

**Q12. Name two ways the AI-guided ablation studies could mislead if read carelessly.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Reading a strategy trial as proof that the algorithm finds the true mechanism, when it tests the
whole approach against PVI [@deisenhofer2025]. And reading a single-arm study's success rate without
its exclusions: in the repeat-procedure study many enrolled patients left before the endpoint, for
example with reconnected veins [@hummel2026], so the rate applies to those who remained.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab builds graph layers on a mesh, trains a graph network to find slow regions on synthetic
maps, deals with rare targets, and then checks a placement classifier on real intracardiac
recordings with honest splits. It runs in under a minute, plus downloads.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Build $\hat A$ on a mesh; check @eq-m39-gcn and @eq-m39-smoothing; smooth a noisy map | synthetic |
| B | Synthetic mapping cases with slow regions; per-point features | synthetic |
| C | A per-point model against a NumPy graph network; ROC AUC, PR AUC, Dice and centroid distance | synthetic |
| D | Rare targets: cross-entropy, weighted cross-entropy and focal loss (@eq-m39-focal) | synthetic |
| E | Catheter position from electrogram features: window-wise against leave-one-patient-out | PhysioNet |
| F | Optional: the graph network in PyTorch | synthetic |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m39_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m39_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m39_lab.ipynb).
- **Data for part E:** the 32 records of the Intracardiac Atrial Fibrillation Database (8 patients,
  a decapolar catheter in 4 positions each) [@iafdb; @goldberger2000], Open Data Commons Attribution v1.0, downloaded
  from PhysioNet and checked against its published SHA-256 list. Without internet access, part E is
  skipped.
- **Part F** runs only if PyTorch is installed.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A vertex has 6 neighbours, and each neighbour also has 6. What is $\hat A_{ij}$ for a
neighbour, and for the vertex itself?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\tilde d = 7$ for all of them, so $\hat A_{ij} = 1/7$ for each neighbour and for itself (@eq-m39-gcn):
a plain average of 7 values.

</details>

**S2. After 3 layers on a grid with 2-mm spacing, how far along the grid lines can information
travel?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

3 edges, so 6 mm along grid lines (diagonal edges reach a little further).

</details>

**S3. Prediction and truth are the same disc. Dice?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1 (@eq-m39-dice).

</details>

**S4. Two discs of radius 3 mm, centres 6 mm apart. Dice?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0: they touch at one point, since $d = R + r$ (@eq-m39-lens).

</details>

**S5. With $\gamma = 0$ and $\alpha = 0.5$, what is the focal loss?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Half the ordinary cross-entropy (@eq-m39-focal).

</details>

**S6. True or false: a window-wise split and a patient-wise split estimate the same thing.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. The window-wise split estimates performance on new windows from patients already seen; the
patient-wise split estimates performance on new patients, which is what matters for use.

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **What the network looked at.** Alhusseini and colleagues, the gradient-weighted class
  activation (Grad-CAM) heatmaps, which they compared with the consensus of expert raters
  [@alhusseini2020; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7438307/)]. This
  module: From the field; interview Q10.
- **A neighbourhood of electrodes.** Zolotarev and colleagues, the figure showing how features are
  averaged over the 8 electrodes around each electrode of a 3-by-3 grid [@zolotarev2020;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7577986/)]. Compare with one unweighted
  graph layer (@eq-m39-gcn, interview Q7).
- **Two endpoints, two answers.** Deisenhofer and colleagues, the Kaplan–Meier curves for freedom
  from AF and from any atrial arrhythmia [@deisenhofer2025;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12003177/)]. Compare the two endpoints
  (clinical correlate).

- **Methods.** @kipf2017 (graph convolutional networks), @lin2017focal (focal loss).
- **Electrogram learning.** @alhusseini2020, @zolotarev2020, @guler2026, @rodrigo2022 (m38).
- **Maps.** @saluja2024 (graph network), @huttelmaier2026 (mixtures on voltage).
- **Outcome prediction.** @tang2022 and @ganesan2025, from Stanford registries.
- **Dispersion and trials.** @seitz2017, @deisenhofer2025 and its follow-ups
  [@deisenhofer2025women; @deisenhofer2025at], @hummel2026.
- **AI competency areas.** Machine learning; graphical models (graph structure on the mapping mesh, without a
  probabilistic model). See the [AI competency map](../ai-competencies.qmd).
